Using a clinic protocol on home readings is our choice and must be said on the slide.
73	
74	Why it matters: SMARThealth India (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].
75	
76	**The kit-built quality clip** (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F16, D2-02-F17]). An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff and the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once and the clip stores that posture. It then enforces 300 seconds of still rest (restarting on movement), checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture, requires stillness through a 60-second measurement, and enforces 60 seconds between readings. A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2). It shows green or red and posts reasons, joined to the reading by time. Legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, bladder and smoking go into a 4-question phone checklist. Thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE.
77	
78	![The reading-quality clip on the upper arm and forearm, with its green and red states](adaptive-care-pictures/13-reading-quality-clip.png)
79	*The kit-built clip checks rest, stillness and arm position; it does not measure blood pressure.*
80	
81	So what for us (OUR VIEW): the engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.
82	
83	### Algorithms that set a dose
84	
85	Four families of dose algorithm are in use; each is bounded.
86	
87	**Closed-loop insulin, the model case.** Control-IQ (randomised 2:1, 168 people with type 1 diabetes, USA, 6 months, against a sensor-augmented pump) raised time in the target glucose range by 11 points and cut HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) by 0.33, with one ketoacidosis case [D1-01-F24]. In insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, 2IQP (randomised 2:1, 319 adults, US and Canada, 13 weeks, both arms on a glucose sensor, maker-funded) cut HbA1c a further 0.6 points [D1-01-F43]. The do-it-yourself system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down [D2-03-F46]:
88	- It acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the core version "cannot issue insulin boluses".
89	- The temporary rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate".
90	- Missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan.
91	
92	Its code (oref0, MIT) says it is "not a 'set and forget' system" [D1-06-F12]; dosing logic sits in `determine-basal.js` [D1-06-F53].
93	
94	**Insulin titration rules.** ADA 2025: start basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, "increase 2 units every 3 days to reach FPG target without hypoglycemia", and if low sugar has no clear reason "lower dose by 10-20%" [D1-06-F16]. An upper limit of 0.5 units/kg/day is quoted (search summary only) [D1-06-F18]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. d-Nav (randomised, 181 adults with type 2 diabetes, 3 US centres, 6 months, device plus clinician against clinician alone) cut HbA1c 1.0% against 0.3% with equal low-sugar events; several authors were maker staff or shareholders [D1-01-F13]. TeleDiab-2 (randomised, 191 adults starting basal insulin, France, 4 months) cut HbA1c 1.44% and 1.48% against 0.92% [D1-01-F14]. The FDA has cleared dose apps such as My Dose Coach (2017) and iSage Rx (2024) [D2-03-F47]. A reinforcement-learning model, RL-DITR, was tested only single-arm in 16 inpatients in China [D2-03-F11].
95	
96	**Blood-pressure protocols.** Gujarat's ladder, with 30-day reviews: amlodipine 5 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, add telmisartan 40 mg, telmisartan 80 mg (after blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein; if any is abnormal, refer, or, with no specialist reachable, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone), add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, then check adherence and refer; the sheet covers adults over 30, checks adherence at each visit, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception [D1-06-F14]. Punjab and Maharashtra differ at step 2 [D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]; across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82% [D1-06-F04]. People do differ: PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden, 1,468 treatment periods) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].
97	
98	**Warfarin tables.** The IWPC algorithm sets only the starting dose [D2-03-F48]. Feedback tables agree on no change at INR (a clotting test) 2.0-3.0 but differ outside it (search summary only) [D1-06-F37]. Self-management cut clots (RR 0.47) and deaths (RR 0.55) in pooled trials, compared indirectly with self-testing [D1-02-F05].
99	
100	| Algorithm | Input | Output | How it is bounded |
101	|---|---|---|---|
102	| Closed-loop insulin | Continuous glucose sensor | Temporary basal rate | Rate caps, no boluses (oref0), revert on missing data [D2-03-F46] |
103	| Basal titration | Fasting glucose over 3 days | +2 units or -10-20% | Upper limit per kg; hypo branch; clinician sets cause [D1-06-F16, D1-06-F18] |
104	| BP ladder | 30-day review of readings | Next written regimen | Fixed steps, lab and pregnancy guards, referral at the end [D1-06-F14] |
105	| Warfarin table | INR | Weekly dose change in % | No-change band 2.0-3.0; hold at high INR [D1-06-F37] |
106	
107	So what for us (OUR VIEW): every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing. A ladder is the simplest case. PHYSIC is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value.
108	
109	### A protocol as data
110	
111	A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch, and swapped without changing the engine. This section gives the prior art, what Indian decision-support trials found, and how our files fit.
112	
113	**Prior art.** A 2002 review of 11 guideline languages found four basic parts: data collection, decision, patient state, intervention [D2-03-F54]. WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit; the blood-pressure kit is for pregnancy only, its machine-readable layers are "not yet available", and its licence is non-commercial [D2-03-F50, D2-03-F51]. HL7 CQL is a standard logic language with an Apache-2.0 engine that is "not a complete implementation" and needs a Java 17 translator [D2-03-F52]. CDS Hooks returns suggestion cards with an accept button (CC BY 4.0) [D2-03-F53]. India's open Simple app (MIT, alive 4 Nov 2026) stores a protocol as a drug list plus `follow_up_days`; no step logic was found in its protocol model [D1-06-F40].
114	
115	**Indian decision-support trials.**
116	
117	| Trial | Design and setting | Compared | Result |
118	|---|---|---|---|
119	| CARRS [D2-03-F14] | Randomised, 1,146 with diabetes, urban clinics, India and Pakistan, 28 months | Coordinators plus decision-support records against usual care | Positive: composite goal 18.2% against 8.1% |
120	| mWellcare [D2-03-F15] | Cluster randomised, 40 health centres, 3,698 people, 12 months | Nurse-run app with decision support against enhanced usual care | Null: systolic -0.98 (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67) |
121	| mPower Heart [D2-03-F16] | Before-and-after, no control, Himachal Pradesh, 6,797 people | Phone tool drafts prescription, physician vets | Systolic -14.6 mmHg, uncontrolled |
122	| SMARThealth India [D2-03-F17] | Stepped-wedge cluster, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh | Health-worker tablet plus doctor decision support against usual care | Null on blood pressure |
123	| IMPACT Diabetes [D2-03-F18] | Cluster randomised, 8 centres, 418 people, 9 months | Health-worker decision support under physician supervision | Small positive: HbA1c fall of 0.5% or more, 21.8% against 10.3% |
124	
125	**The test-coverage lesson.** When the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].
126	
127	**How our files fit** (OUR DESIGN, detail in part J). One YAML file per protocol (Gujarat, Nigeria, and the ADA insulin rule as paper only), each number carrying the exact source words; a missing value is `null` and the engine refuses that branch [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15, D1-06-F16]. A pure `decide()` function checks safety first, then enough readings, the 30-day interval, the threshold, adherence, the last step, and the lab and pregnancy guards, and only then proposes a step. It never computes a dose; it only picks a regimen written in the file. Thirty-six test cases cover every branch listed so far, run against two protocols; the age, childbearing-age, abnormal-lab and "outside the demo" branches found later on the sheets still need tests (part J) [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15].
128	
129	So what for us (OUR VIEW): decision support alone did not beat a well-run programme in two Indian trials, so our engine must act between visits, not prompt during them. ATHENA's 1% says to test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.

131	### Adaptive nudging, bandits and reinforcement learning
132	
133	Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. A just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) adapts "weekly, daily, or even many times a day"; a micro-randomised trial randomises each decision point [D2-03-F01].
134	
135	| Study | Design | Result |
136	|---|---|---|
137	| HeartSteps V1 [D2-03-F02] | Micro-randomised, 44 US adults, 6 weeks | Any suggestion +35 steps in 30 minutes (p = .06), fading over time; walking suggestions +59 (p = .02) |
138	| HeartSteps V2 [D2-03-F03]; Oralytics [D2-03-F08] | Learning algorithms deployed in US trials | Outcome results NOT FOUND |
139	| DIAMANTE [D2-03-F10] | Randomised, 3 arms, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months | Learned texts beat random texts: steps up 19% against 1.6% (random) and 3.9% (weekly message); HbA1c not in the abstract |
140	| Automated diabetes prevention app [D2-03-F42] | Randomised non-inferiority, 368 people, 2 US sites, 12 months | Matched human coaches: 31.7% against 31.9% |
141	| JITAI meta-analyses [D2-03-F04, D2-03-F06] | Mental health, 23 studies; sleep, 11 trials | Small effect (g = 0.15); adaptive not better than non-adaptive for sleep |
142	
143	Two cautions. Standard estimators "can be inconsistent and fail to be replicable" on bandit-trial data [D2-03-F09]. A 2026 guideline for live learning systems uses pre-set fallbacks, which "safeguarded participants" in two case studies [D2-03-F07].
144	
145	Open tools: MABWiser (Apache 2.0) [D1-06-F55]; Open Bandit Pipeline (Apache 2.0, off-policy estimators) [D2-03-F49]; HeartSteps V1 data (CC BY 4.0, 8,274 decisions) [D1-06-F44].
146	
147	So what for us (OUR VIEW): adaptive timing has one head-to-head win, on steps, not a clinical measure. In our loop it could help complete 7-day reading blocks, later. A HeartSteps replay shows the method only.
148	
149	### Personal response models and "digital twins"
150	
151	A "digital twin" here is a model of one person that predicts their response to food or treatment.
152	
153	- **Twin Health, India, blood pressure** [D2-03-F19]: secondary analysis of an Indian randomised trial in 319 people with type 2 diabetes (233 twin, 86 standard care). Home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes. Systolic fell 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg at one year. Limits: secondary analysis, only 59 people on blood-pressure drugs, company-linked. The drug changes followed a protocol; the machine learning predicted diet response.
154	- **Method** [D2-03-F21]: predicts each person's post-meal glucose from a glucose sensor, food logs and other inputs and "dynamically adjusts dietary recommendations". No open code found.
155	- **Twin Health, US** [D2-03-F43]: randomised, 150 people, Cleveland Clinic, 12 months; HbA1c under 6.5% without glucose drugs other than metformin in 71% against 2.4%. Source is the institution's summary; funding not shown.
156	- **Twin Health, real world** [D2-03-F20]: 1,853 completers, HbA1c -1.8%, no control (THEIR CLAIM).
157	- **Glucose foundation models**: GluFormer (over 10 million readings, 10,812 adults) predicted later diabetes and cardiovascular death (arXiv only) [D2-03-F23]; CGM-LSM and GlucoFM report lower forecast error [D2-03-F24].
158	- **Blood pressure**: one agent-based model simulates six drugs on virtual patients; licence unconfirmed (search summary only) [D1-06-F43].
159	
160	PHYSIC measured personal response over repeated periods [D2-03-F12]; a single run-in response did not predict the long-term one [D2-03-F13].
161	
162	So what for us (OUR VIEW): no open twin exists for blood-pressure drugs. Each approved step in our loop gives one labelled example (readings before, readings 30 days after). That is the dataset a response model would need, and it does not exist in the open today [D1-06-F42].

185	
186	Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol.

188	| Study | Setup | Error |
189	|---|---|---|

191	| Anticoagulant hold times [D2-03-F39] | ChatGPT and Gemini, 25 cases | "potentially dangerous recommendations in 12-20% of scenarios" |

194	
195	No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44], and an Indian trial protocol uses a frozen Mistral-7B with nurses after heart surgery [D2-03-F37].
196	
197	**The design pattern** (OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]):
198	1. The model handles language only: cuff photo to strict JSON, translation, speech.
199	2. A fixed, tested engine makes every decision, from the protocol file.
200	3. Code checks every output against the protocol: plausible ranges, two agreeing reads, a regimen that exists in the file.
201	4. A clinician approves every change.

270	### So what for us
271	
272	OUR VIEW.
273	- **The reading is the science.** Arm position alone adds 3.9-6.5 mmHg [D2-02-F16], and noisy readings broke an Indian trial [D2-03-F17]. The clip and reading rules are our deep-tech claim, not the rules engine.
274	- **Bound every action.** Copy OpenAPS [D2-03-F46]: choose only written regimens, hold the current step on missing data, never step on one reading.
275	- **Keep models on language.** A constrained model still made dangerous dose errors 1% of the time [D2-03-F38]; it reads photos and speaks Hindi, and the engine decides.
276	- **Act between visits, not during them.** Decision support used during clinic visits did not beat good usual care in India [D2-03-F15, D2-03-F17]; our value is the change made without a visit.
277	- **The learning layer is earned, not claimed.** People do respond differently to drugs [D2-03-F12], but no open data exists to model it; each approved step we log builds it.

177	### The gap
178	
179	OUR VIEW. No Indian service was found that turns home BP or glucose readings into a medicine change between visits [D1-04-F09, D1-04-F19]. Indian programmes stop at coaching or reminders [D1-04-F02, D1-06-F40]. Abroad the space is held by US programmes paid by US payers [D1-05-F13, D1-05-F46]; the low-income-country programmes found are protocol care, not device-linked dose loops [D1-05-F65]. The closest abroad: Closed Loop Medicine (UK) has been in members' voluntary liquidation since 28 Apr 2026 [D3-06-F07], its website now points to a licensing firm [D3-06-F08], and its one trial had no comparison group (205 patients, systolic down 11 mmHg) [D3-06-F09]; Cadence's protocol-bound titration software entered a US regulator's (FDA) pilot on 13 Aug 2026 and is not cleared (THEIR CLAIM) [D3-06-F31]; and Omron, the Japanese cuff maker, has a UK product that drafts a medication plan for the clinician to accept or modify (search summary only) [D3-06-F35]. These are one night's search results: a hospital, drug maker or state may run something unpublished.
180	
181	### So what for us
182	
183	OUR VIEW.
184	- **Stand where nobody was found:** a home BP loop that proposes the next protocol step for a doctor to approve, the only kind of programme PHTI passed [D1-05-F2].
185	- **Sell to a payer, not a patient.** Pear, Akili and Better Therapeutics had trials yet failed for lack of payment [D1-05-F20, D1-02-F44, D1-02-F46].
186	- **Build the prescriber in.** Clinician referral adds 40 days of retention [D1-02-F27]; Pear lacked prescribers [D1-05-F21].
187	- **Never sell the sensor or the reminder as the product,** and keep spending in line with revenue [D1-02-F41, D1-04-F23].
188	- **Measure what payers count from day one:** share under 140/90, and how many lost patients return [D1-05-F31].

159	- **Money goes to AI clinician time and virtual clinics.** The largest rounds are Function $298M, Hippocratic AI $126M, Cadence $100M and Nourish $100M [D2-06-F42, D2-06-F20, D2-06-F1, D2-06-F5]; only Cadence describes medicine changes.

Consumers pay only for tests and companions, Function at $365 a year and Bevel at $6 a month [D2-06-F43, D2-06-F33]; none of those changes a dose. 165	### 7. Eight ideas to borrow for a home blood-pressure step loop
166	
167	OUR VIEW, most useful first.
168	
169	1. Protocol held as data, options with reasons shown to the clinician, response fed back (Closed Loop Medicine) [D2-06-F24].
170	2. Before any step up, a call in the patient's language asks whether the tablet was taken, as the Gujarat protocol requires (Tucuvi) [D2-06-F10, D1-06-F14].
171	3. Report readings closed with no clinician touch and clinician minutes per patient (Cadence) [D2-06-F2].
172	4. Log every accept, edit and reject as the safety and training record (Counsel Health) [D2-06-F11].
173	5. A one-page staged safety ladder: supervised first, wider authority after testing (Hippocratic AI) [D2-06-F20].
174	6. Alert on drift of the 7-day mean, not single readings (Prana) [D2-06-F13].
175	7. One reading schema (value, time, device, quality) for any cuff or watch (Junction) [D2-06-F30].
176	8. Cuffless or 24-hour readings as an input or one-off check only; dose decisions stay on cuff readings (Aktiia, Biobeat) [D2-06-F37, D2-06-F36].

41	| Insurers | 58.20 crore lives under 2.65 crore policies in 2024-25 [D2-05-F08]. FY25 health premiums ₹1,27,417 crore (Outlook Money) or ₹1,17,505 crore (ORF, 21 Jan 2026); the two may measure different things [D2-05-F09]. Outpatient cover below 0.1% of a US$37.7 billion outpatient market (industry-sponsored, search summary only) [D2-05-F10]. IRDAI's 2024 master circular says insurers should offer products covering chronic conditions and outpatient care; it does not mandate them [D2-04-F33]. Insurance-linked firms are buying care firms: PB Health (PB Fintech) bought Fitterfly in Nov 2025 [D2-05-F35]. | Not yet: almost no outpatient cover. Their care arms are the opening. |
42	| Employers | could not be confirmed | Possible, with a slow sales cycle. |
43	| State programmes | 42.01 million hypertension patients put on standard care by the public programme, as of 5 Mar 2025 (search summary only; three outlets agree) [D1-03-F14]. Medicines about ₹200 a patient a year [D2-01-F12]. AB-PMJAY pays ₹5 lakh per family a year for hospital care only (search summary only); outpatient chronic care runs through Ayushman Arogya Mandirs and 6,410 NCD clinics [D2-04-F47]. Full programme cost per patient NOT FOUND; state purchases of digital health NOT FOUND [D2-05-F18]. | Largest pool, lowest price; only for proven results. |
44	
45	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** The first payer is a private clinic or hospital chain. Insurers become a payer only after outcome data exist.
46	
47	### 4. Market size, counted two ways
48	
49	![Market size, counted two ways](adaptive-care-pictures/23-market-size.png)
50	*Chart: the levels used after counting each two ways. OUR ARITHMETIC; several inputs are assumptions.*
51	
52	All figures here are OUR ARITHMETIC from our market model (DT3), in rupees a year, at ₹149 a patient a month, ₹1,788 a year (ASSUMPTION, from the build plan). Each level is counted top-down and bottom-up, and the lower figure is used so the case does not rest on the kinder count.
53	
54	| Level | Top-down | Bottom-up | Used (the lower) |
55	|---|---|---|---|
56	| TAM: every Indian adult on blood-pressure medicines who could be served (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹7,494 crore (419.1 lakh private retail patients) | ₹9,969 crore (557.5 lakh treated adults, low case) | **₹7,494 crore** |
57	| SAM: private patients a doctor could enrol on a household smartphone (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹1,668 crore (93.3 lakh patients through 3.1 lakh doctors) | ₹749 crore (41.9 lakh patients) | **₹749 crore** |
58	| SOM year 3 (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹3.7 crore (0.5% of SAM) | ₹2.1 crore (60 clinics x 200 patients) | **₹2.1 crore** |
59	| SOM year 5 (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹22.5 crore (3% of SAM) | ₹17.9 crore (400 clinics x 250 patients) | **₹17.9 crore** |
60	
61	(TAM: total market; SAM: the part we could serve; SOM: the part we could win.)
62	
63	**How each figure is counted.**
64	- **TAM top-down.** Retail blood-pressure medicine sales ₹16,371 crore [D2-05-F01] divided by a private patient's yearly medicine spend ₹3,906 [D2-05-F17] = 419.1 lakh patients buying in the private market. Times ₹1,788 a year = ₹7,494 crore. The spend figure is a modelled price for one brand pill a day; across the paper's range of about ₹2,500 to ₹5,100 the count runs from 321.0 lakh to 654.8 lakh patients [D2-05-F17].
65	- **TAM bottom-up.** 315 million adults with high blood pressure (a 2021 projection by the survey's investigators, not a count) [D1-03-F02] x 17.7% on medicines (NFHS-5 2019-21, preprint) [D1-03-F07] = 557.5 lakh (the ceiling from drug sales, 30.7%, a 2018 ceiling that assumes the public sector gives 30% of treatment [D2-05-F30], would give 967.0 lakh). Times ₹1,788 = ₹9,969 crore.
66	- **SAM bottom-up.** 419.1 lakh private patients x 50% reachable on a household smartphone x 20% whose doctor could enrol them (both ASSUMPTION) = 41.9 lakh patients. Times ₹1,788 = ₹749 crore.
67	- **SAM top-down.** 13,88,185 registered doctors (reply to Parliament, December 2025) [D2-05-F38] x 80% in practice x 70% private x 40% managing blood pressure = 3.1 lakh doctors, x 30 patients each = 93.3 lakh patients. Times ₹1,788 = ₹1,668 crore. The 80% is the ministry's own availability assumption, for allopathic and AYUSH doctors together; the rest are ASSUMPTION. Beside our 70% private: the notes have 11% of registered doctors in government in 2018, and "more than 80%" private in an NSSO-based study (search summary only) [D3-07-F08]. The model has not been rerun with these.
68	- **SOM bottom-up.** Clinics live and paying patients per clinic at each year end; the first year is an unpaid pilot (all ASSUMPTION):
69	
70	| Year | Clinics | Patients per clinic | Paying patients | Revenue a year |
71	|---|---|---|---|---|
72	| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | pilot, unpaid |
73	| 2 | 15 | 150 | 2,250 | ₹0.4 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
74	| 3 | 60 | 200 | 12,000 | ₹2.1 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
75	| 4 | 180 | 220 | 39,600 | ₹7.1 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
76	| 5 | 400 | 250 | 1,00,000 | ₹17.9 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
77	
78	The model leaves out public-system patients (shown in section 6), diabetes and other conditions, device sales and every country outside India.
79	
80	**The weakest inputs.** The smartphone and enrolment shares (50% and 20%) are guesses, and they set the SAM used; the 50% is in line with smartphone access of 57.9% at ages 50-59 and 44.7% at 60-69 (quoted second-hand) [D3-07-F11]. The 17.7% treated share rests on a preprint: 17.7% of all adults with hypertension treated, NFHS-5, 2019-21 [D1-03-F07]. The private count comes from medicine sales because no measured hypertension split exists; the 30.7% ceiling is built on an assumed 30% public share [D2-05-F30, D3-07-F04].
81	
82	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** The used SAM of ₹749 crore is real money but small for a venture fund. The year-5 figure of ₹17.9 crore depends entirely on how fast clinics sign.
83	
84	### 5. The US$100 million-a-year test
85	
86	The test asks whether the company could reach US$100 million of revenue a year.
87	
88	- US$100 million a year = ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026) (OUR ARITHMETIC).
89	- At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients (52,71,253) (OUR ARITHMETIC).
90	- The serviceable market above holds 41.9 lakh patients. **The test fails on this model in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (OUR ARITHMETIC).
91	
92	At higher prices fewer patients are needed: 7,85,417 at ₹1,000 a month, 3,92,708 at ₹2,000, and 3,40,136 at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month (revenue over all members, not a price) (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹9,42,50,00,000 divided by the yearly price) [D2-05-F23].
93	
94	Where the rest would have to come from: more protocols on the same loop (diabetes, heart failure), a paid public tier, other countries that use the same family of protocols, or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.
95	
96	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company. The pitch must show the same engine carrying more protocols and more payers.
97	
98	### 6. Price sensitivity and the public tier
99	
100	The model at three prices (OUR ARITHMETIC; prices are ASSUMPTION).
101	
102	| Price a month | SAM used | SOM year 5 (bottom-up) | Patients needed for US$100 million |
103	|---|---|---|---|
104	| ₹99 | ₹498 crore | ₹11.9 crore | 79.3 lakh (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
105	| ₹149 | ₹749 crore | ₹17.9 crore | 52.7 lakh (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
106	| ₹299 | ₹1,504 crore | ₹35.9 crore | 26.3 lakh (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
107	
108	**A public tier, shown apart.** 420.1 lakh patients on treatment in the public programme [D1-03-F14] x ₹15 a month (ASSUMPTION) x 12 = ₹756 crore a year (OUR ARITHMETIC). A state would pay this only for results, since the medicines themselves cost about ₹200 a patient a year [D2-01-F12].
109	
110	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Price moves the result as much as clinic count. The public tier matches the private SAM but needs outcome proof first.
111	
112	### 7. Unit economics per patient a month
113	
114	From the build note (D2-01, section 6). Every cost line is an ASSUMPTION to be checked.
115	
116	| Line | Value | Label |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| Price to clinic, private tier | ₹149 per active patient a month | ASSUMPTION; below Sugar.fit's ₹2,499 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹29,990 / 12) [D1-04-F04] |
119	| Messages | ₹15 (WhatsApp templates; Telegram is ₹0). Two resellers copying Meta's India card give ₹0.115 a utility message and ₹0.8631 a marketing message, before 18% GST, from 1 Oct 2026 (third party, not Meta) [D3-07-F20, D3-07-F21] | ASSUMPTION |
120	| Cloud and storage | ₹5 | ASSUMPTION |
121	| Reading cuff photos | ₹2 (about 30 photos) | ASSUMPTION |
122	| Health-worker call to silent patients | ₹30 (one 5-minute call a month; ₹25,000 salary / 9,600 call-minutes x 5 = about ₹13, rounded up for overhead) | ASSUMPTION and OUR ARITHMETIC |
123	| Doctor time | 6.5-8.5 proposals per 100 patients a month at 30 seconds each, about 4 minutes per 100 patients; not costed | OUR SIMULATION and ASSUMPTION |
124	| **Gross margin** | **₹149 - (15 + 5 + 2 + 30) = ₹97, about 65%** | **OUR ARITHMETIC** |
125	| Cuff | ₹2,600 one time (search summary only) [D1-06-F31], or the patient's own | paid by patient or clinic |
126	
127	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** The health-worker call is the largest cost. The margin holds only if doctors approve proposals without being paid per approval.
128	
129	### 8. What comparable companies earn and are worth
130	
131	Indian chronic-care firms in the notes lose money; the profitable foreign ones are paid by employers and plans.
132	
133	| Company | Revenue and result | Funding, value, exit | Source |
134	|---|---|---|---|
135	| Sugar.fit (India) | FY25 ₹66.5 crore (+77%), loss ₹42 crore | not in these notes | [D2-05-F19] |
136	| BeatO (India) | revenue could not be confirmed (the one page found contradicts itself) | US$47.6M+ raised; last round Nov 2022 | [D2-05-F20] |
137	| Fitterfly (India) | could not be confirmed | raised about US$18.9M, last valued US$41.7M; bought by PB Health, Nov 2025, price undisclosed | [D2-05-F35] |
138	| Healthify (India) | FY23 ₹228.76 crore, loss ₹142 crore; FY24 about ₹206.3 crore, loss about ₹88 crore (aggregators) | US$20M Series D, Oct 2024; US$550M third-party value | [D2-05-F22] |
139	| Wellthy (India) | NOT FOUND | bought by TruDoc, 13 Feb 2024, price undisclosed | [D2-05-F14] |
140	| Omada (US) | Q3 2026 US$91.3M, 1,134,000 members, net income US$6.551M; revenue per member US$294 a year, about US$24.5 a month (OUR ARITHMETIC: 294 / 12), gross margin 76% (both in the company's Q3 release) | listed; one partner group US$53.7M or US$57.7M of the quarter (two sources) | [D1-05-F12, D1-05-F13, D2-05-F23] |
141	| Hinge Health (US) | Q3 2026 US$234.97M, net income US$57.398M | listed; mainly self-insured employers | [D1-05-F15, D1-05-F16] |
142	| Twin Health (US) | revenue NOT FOUND (aggregator estimates conflict, US$1M to US$250M) | US$53M Series E at about US$950M (Aug 2025) | [D2-05-F15, D1-05-F48] |
143	| Cadence (US) | price NOT FOUND | US$100M Series C, June 2026 (reported 23 and 24 Jun) | [D2-05-F24, D1-05-F46] |
144	
145	No US medicine-adjusting programme publishes a price per member a month. Cadence claims US$1,302 a patient a year lower total cost of care (THEIR CLAIM) [D1-05-F46]. The Medicare remote-monitoring benchmark is about US$100 a patient a month in older industry articles (search summary only) [D2-05-F24].
146	
147	**Cost-effectiveness.** TASMINH2 (UK, self-titration against usual care, a 35-year model, 2014): about £1,624 per QALY (a year of life in full health) for men and £4,923 for women, if the blood-pressure gain lasts 2 years for men and 5 for women (SOURCE ESTIMATE) [D2-05-F25]. TASMINH4 (UK, 2019): £17,424 per QALY, 89% likely cost-effective at £20,000 (search summary only) [D2-05-F26]. No Indian study was found.
148	
149	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** About US$24.5 of revenue a member a month is reached abroad only with employer and insurer payers. Indian comparables are small, loss-making and sold at undisclosed prices.
150	
151	### 9. The funding climate in 2026
152	
153	- US digital health raised US$7.4 billion in 244 deals in H1 2026, against US$6.4 billion in H1 2025; deals of US$100 million or more took 45% [D2-05-F16].
154	- India health-tech raised US$310 million in H1 2026 (headline only, tracker not named) [D2-05-F11].
155	- All Indian tech start-ups raised US$7.2 billion in H1 2026, up 12%, with fewer deals (search summary only) [D2-05-F13].
156	
157	### 10. The rules in India
158	
159	These are readings of the texts; open points remain questions for a lawyer and for CDSCO (the national medical-device regulator).
160	
161	**(a) Software as a medical device.** CDSCO issued its "Guidance Document on Medical Device Software" (CDSCO/MD/GD/MDSW/01/2026) on 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01]. Class follows the intended use, as stated in the label, website and promotion [D2-04-F02]. Its grid for standalone software [D2-04-F03]:
162	
163	| Situation | Treatment or diagnosis | Drive clinical management | Inform clinical management |
164	|---|---|---|---|
165	| Critical | D | C | B |
166	| Serious | C | B | A |
167	| Non-serious | B | A | A |
168	
169	"Drive clinical management" covers information "to guide next diagnostics or next treatment interventions" and support for "safe and effective use of medicinal products" [D2-04-F04]. A dose proposal a doctor approves reads most naturally as "drive": Class B if hypertension is "serious", Class A if "non-serious", Class C if CDSCO reads it as "treatment" [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F49]. The guidance does not say where hypertension sits, so the class turns on that grading [D2-04-F05]. A patient-facing tool used without a professional can be moved up to "critical" [D2-04-F03]. CDSCO names a hypertension digital therapeutics platform and a Bluetooth cuff app as medical device software, and bars the wellness carve-out once a disease is named [D2-04-F07, D2-04-F09]. Unlike the US, there is no exemption for tools only a clinician sees [D2-04-F10]. CDSCO confirms the class on review [D2-04-F06].
170	
171	**(b) A study on patients before a licence.** A test licence (Form MD-13) covers making small quantities "for the purpose of Clinical Investigations or Test or Evaluation or Demonstration" [D2-04-F13]. A clinical investigation on patients needs CDSCO permission (MD-22/MD-23) [D2-04-F14]; the flowchart notes it is not mandatory for Class A [D2-04-F39]. A desk test on open data, simulators or teammates is not a clinical investigation; whether a pilot where software drafts and a doctor decides counts as one is a question for counsel [D2-04-F50]. Fees and processing days NOT FOUND [D2-04-F16].
172	
173	**(c) Telemedicine.** The Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (25 Mar 2020), clause 5.4, say platforms based on artificial intelligence or machine learning "are not allowed to counsel the patients or prescribe any medicines"; such tools may "assist and support" the doctor, but only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and "the final prescription or counseling has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner) [D2-04-F17]. List B medicines may be added at a follow-up; the guidelines define follow-up as the same doctor, same condition, within 6 months of the previous in-person consultation (clause 3.6.2) [D2-04-F17, D2-01-F10]. Annexure 1 names hypertension examples (List A refills such as enalapril and atenolol; List B add-on of a thiazide diuretic with atenolol); amlodipine, telmisartan and chlorthalidone are not named [D2-04-F17]. The claims check read the official text; whether later rules changed it in 2026 was not checked [D2-04-F17].
174	
175	**(d) Nurse or health officer changing a dose.** In the national hypertension programme, community health officers delivered refills "based on the patient's prior prescription"; no titration by them is described [D2-04-F18]. NOT FOUND: any law, rule or ministry order letting a nurse, health officer or pharmacist change a dose under a standing order [D2-04-F18].
176	
177	**(e) Claims and advertising.** The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 bans advertisements suggesting a drug treats a disease in its Schedule, which lists "Diabetes", "Heart diseases" and "High or low blood pressure" [D2-04-F31]. Whether software counts as a "drug" under it is untested; a question for counsel [D2-04-F31].
178	
179	**(f) Data law.** Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules 2025, consent-manager rules start one year after 13 Nov 2025, on 13 Nov 2026; notice, consent and data-fiduciary duties start 18 months after, on 13 May 2027, by the gazette's wording; one law firm (AZB) says a day earlier, 12 Nov 2026 and 12 May 2027 [D2-04-F19, D2-04-F20]. Health data has no general exemption; only children's-data duties are waived for health providers [D2-04-F40].
180	
181	**(g) Ethics and registration.** ICMR's 2023 AI guidelines say humans should keep "complete control" and require consent that names the AI [D2-04-F35]. Trial registration on CTRI is mandatory before first enrolment for trials, with ethics approval uploaded; whether a clinician-decides pilot needs it is NOT FOUND (search summary only) [D2-04-F45].
182	
183	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Clinician sign-off lowers the class; it does not take the software out of the device rules.
184	
185	### 11. The rules and payment abroad
186	
187	Each country has a device route and a payment route; none fits our loop exactly.
188	
189	| | Device rule | How it is paid | NOT FOUND |
190	|---|---|---|---|
191	| United States | Insulin-titration software is a Class II device cleared by 510(k): My Dose Coach (K163099, K171230), d-Nav (K181916) [D2-04-F24]. Software is not a device if it supports a clinician who can review its basis and does not analyse a device signal [D2-04-F22]; FDA's 6 Jan 2026 guidance extends this to a single recommendation, for clinician-facing tools only [D2-04-F23]. Whether home cuff readings count as a signal is a question for counsel [D2-04-F23]. | Medicare remote monitoring: from 1 Jan 2027 a face-to-face initiating visit is needed; clinical staff must be direct employees from 1 Jan 2029 [D2-04-F26]. Digital therapy codes cover behavioural health only [D2-04-F41]. | A 510(k) for blood-pressure titration software (not searched separately); 2026 payment amounts [D2-04-F24, D2-04-F27] |
192	| Germany | Prescribed-app (DiGA) route: positive care effect required; decision in 3 months; trial listing up to 12 months, extendable by 12 [D2-04-F28]. | Price negotiated after year one; from 1 Jan 2026 at least 20% of the price must depend on measured outcomes [D2-04-F29]. Average negotiated price €227 (search summary only) [D2-04-F42]. | Device-class limit in the statute [D2-04-F30] |
193	| Japan | CureApp HT, a hypertension app, approved Apr 2022 (search summary only) [D2-04-F37] and insured from 1 Sep 2022 as an add-on treatment app that coaches lifestyle (salt, weight, exercise), not a dose change [D3-06-F19]. A 6-month billing cap could not be confirmed. | From 1 Jun 2026: 90 points a month in person or 78 points online (the online rate is new), once a month, plus 7,010 yen for the app as an insured material (company release and a news report) [D2-04-F43, D3-06-F20]; patient pays 30% (search summary only) [D3-06-F20]. | Uptake (clinics, patients) [D2-04-F43] |
194	
195	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** All three pay through a clinician, and Germany now ties part of the price to outcomes.
196	
197	### 12. What tonight's prototype may and may not say
198	
199	OUR VIEW, drawn from section 10:
200	- It is a prototype for test and demonstration, not a medical device on sale and not tested on patients [D2-04-F50].
201	- It uses open data, simulated patients or teammates' readings; no patient data.
202	- A clinician approves every dose change and the doctor directly delivers the prescription and counselling; the software only drafts and shows its reasons [D2-04-F17, D2-04-F35].
203	- It makes no claim that it treats or controls high blood pressure, and no claim of benefit to patients [D2-04-F31].
204	
205	### 13. Three questions for a lawyer
206	
207	From the regulation note [D2-04-F49, D2-04-F50]:
208	1. Under CDSCO's 2026 grid, is a clinician-approved blood-pressure (or insulin) step proposal "drive clinical management" or "treatment or diagnosis", and is essential hypertension "serious" or "non-serious"? Will CDSCO give a written class opinion before we build?
209	2. For a pilot where software drafts and a registered doctor approves each change, do we need a test licence, clinical-investigation permission and CTRI registration, or only ethics approval? Who is the sponsor and the data fiduciary: the clinic, us, or both?
210	3. Under the 2020 telemedicine guidelines and the prescription-drug rules, may an approved change be sent by text as a follow-up consultation, does a message sent in the doctor's name after approval count as the doctor directly delivering the prescription (clause 5.4), and may a nurse or health officer deliver it under a written protocol? Does marketing that names hypertension engage section 3(d) of the 1954 Act?
211	
212	### 14. So what for us
213	
214	OUR VIEW:
215	- Sell to private clinics and hospital chains first, at about ₹149 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION); patients alone will not pay enough.
216	- The used SAM is ₹749 crore and the US$100 million test fails in India on blood pressure alone (OUR ARITHMETIC), so the pitch is one engine for many protocols and payers.
217	- The Indian pilot must produce control data at 90 days, because insurers, states and German-style outcome pay all ask for it.
218	- Plan for Class B, ask CDSCO for a written class early, and keep the doctor approving every change.
219	- Build data consent to the May 2027 duties now, and say nothing in public about treating blood pressure.

23:- **The engine.** One pure Python function, `decide()`, reads a protocol file (YAML, a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with reasons. No input or output, no clock, no randomness. It never computes a dose; it can only pick a regimen written in the file. No language model in the dose path. Stack: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic, pytest.
26:- **The quality clip.** An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff (0x68) and a wrist strap (0x69), on GPIO21 and GPIO22. It enforces 300 seconds of still rest, checks the forearm is near horizontal (within 20 degrees) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of a calibrated posture, holds stillness through each 60-second reading, and posts a valid flag with reasons. It does not measure blood pressure. It targets arm hanging at the side (+6.5/+4.4 mmHg) and arm on the lap (+3.9/+4.0) against arm on a desk, from a crossover randomised trial of 133 adults in Baltimore [D2-02-F16]. Unsensed errors (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking) go into a phone checklist.

#### (c) The decision in plain steps

1. If the patient is referred or waiting for lab results, do nothing. If the patient is outside the sheet's population (30 or under on the Gujarat file), or has diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease, flag "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle [D1-06-F14].
2. Keep only readings that passed the quality gate.
3. Safety first. Newest session at or above 180 systolic or 110 diastolic: ask for a repeat after rest; if confirmed, raise an urgent card and tell the patient to contact the clinic today. This beats the 30-day wait. The low-pressure branch fires only once a clinician sets its threshold.
4. Fewer than 3 valid days: ask for more readings.
5. Fewer than 30 days on the step: "keep going".
6. Home mean below 135/85: "same medicine", no doctor needed.
7. At or above the line: ask the adherence question. Any missed day, or no tablets left: send support, no step-up, card to the clinician for information.
8. On the last step: propose referral.
9. Pregnant, or a woman of childbearing age not on effective contraception, and the next step has a barred drug (telmisartan, chlorthalidone, or any ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide-type diuretic or statin): propose referral. Amlodipine steps may go ahead; uncontrolled on the intensified amlodipine dose: propose referral [D1-06-F14]. Labs missing before telmisartan 80: propose a lab order. Any lab value abnormal: propose referral, or, if no specialist can be reached, propose withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone [D1-06-F14].
10. Otherwise propose the next step, quoting the sheet line. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.

The adherence question is two chat buttons: "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more" and "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no". Adherent means 0 missed days. That cut-off is OUR DESIGN and the clinician can change it, because the sheet says "Check for compliance at each visit before titration of dose or addition of drugs" but gives no number [D1-06-F14].

#### (d) The home-reading rule

- **Block:** on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle, two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-01-F1, D2-02-F10].
- **Valid session:** both readings pass the quality flags; its value is their mean.
- **Enough:** at least 3 distinct valid days, aiming for 7. ESH (the European Society of Hypertension) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-01-F1].
- **Day 1:** dropped only if 4 or more valid days remain. ESH calls dropping it a "matter of debate" [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10].
- **Still high (the home threshold):** mean systolic at or above 135 OR mean diastolic at or above 85. ESH says home 135/85 corresponds to office 140/90 [D2-01-F1]; ISH says home hypertension is readings "consistently 135/85 mm Hg or greater" [D2-01-F3]; the Indian Guidelines IV give above 135/85 (search summary only) [D2-01-F4, D2-02-F15].
- **Very high:** any single session at or above 180 or 110.
- **Clinic reading in the cycle:** the card shows both; the clinician decides.

The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings ("SBP 140 or DBP 90") [D1-06-F14]. **Mapping a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** Say so aloud on the slide, and keep the threshold a protocol value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

#### (e) The test table

25:- **The reading route.** Every route writes {sys, dia, pulse, time, source, quality_flag}. D2-02's order for tonight: a phone photo of any cuff's screen, read by a vision model and confirmed by the patient; an Omron HEM-7156T over Bluetooth with omblepy, only if one is in hand by about 02:00 [D2-02-F1]; typed entry, always built. Photos are read twice, checked for plausible ranges, and shown back for confirmation. Purpose-trained readers reached 0.9-1.2 mmHg mean systolic error on held-out sets, but about 82% of one Guatemalan field set were poor-quality images and errors clustered in the last digit [D2-02-F4]; general vision models are untested on cuff screens [D2-02-F8].

## J. MVP ladder and tonight's build pack

### 1. What this part shows

This part is tonight's build pack and the plan for the two steps after it. It merges the software note (D2-01) and the hardware note (D2-02) into one schedule, one test list and one list of honest claims for noon.

OUR DESIGN, all three rungs:

| Rung | When | What it is | What it proves | What it cannot prove |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Tonight | 23:00 Thu 13 Nov to 12:00 Fri 14 Nov | Engine, three screens, reading route, quality clip, tests, simulation | The code does what the protocol sheet says in every listed branch; readings flow end to end; a person can rule on a card in seconds | Anything about patients |

### 2. Rung 1, tonight

#### (a) What gets built

OUR DESIGN, from the two build notes:

- **The engine.** One pure Python function, `decide()`, reads a protocol file (YAML, a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with reasons. No input or output, no clock, no randomness. It never computes a dose; it can only pick a regimen written in the file. No language model in the dose path. Stack: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic, pytest.
- **Three screens.** (1) Patient: Telegram chat, same flow on a web form as fallback: measure prompt, photo or typed entry, adherence buttons, change message. - **The reading route.** Every route writes {sys, dia, pulse, time, source, quality_flag}. It enforces 300 seconds of still rest, checks the forearm is near horizontal (within 20 degrees) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of a calibrated posture, holds stillness through each 60-second reading, and posts a valid flag with reasons. It does not measure blood pressure. It targets arm hanging at the side (+6.5/+4.4 mmHg) and arm on the lap (+3.9/+4.0) against arm on a desk, from a crossover randomised trial of 133 adults in Baltimore [D2-02-F16]. Unsensed errors (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking) go into a phone checklist.

## Appendix C. The technology in detail

This appendix holds the detail behind chapter 2.3 (and the system parts in chapter 4): for each stage of a therapy loop, the technology that exists in November 2026, its cost and testing, and what a student team can build by noon. The protocol file itself (doses, steps, intervals, thresholds) and tonight's parts list and costs are in Appendix G; here we explain the idea of a protocol as data and the science of a trustworthy home reading. OUR VIEW: the hard engineering is in trusting the home reading and in bounding the decision, not in the model that makes it.

### C1. The parts of a therapy loop

A loop that changes treatment has six stages. The picture of this system map is in chapter 4.

| Stage | Its job | Technology found | Our build tonight (OUR VIEW) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sense | Get a number from the patient's home | Omron cuffs read with omblepy [D1-06-F07]; cuff-screen photo readers [D2-02-F4]; Bluetooth glucose profile [D1-06-F29] | Photo of any cuff, confirmed by the patient; typed entry as fallback |
| Check the reading | Was it taken properly? | AHA and ESH home rules [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F11]; posture-error trials [D2-02-F16] | Kit-built motion clip plus a checklist |
| Decide | Turn valid readings into a proposed next step | Step protocols [D1-06-F14]; HL7 CQL [D2-03-F52]; OpenAPS bounds [D2-03-F46] | One YAML file per protocol, run by a pure `decide()` function |
| Confirm | A clinician accepts or rejects | CDS Hooks cards with an accept button [D2-03-F53] | Clinician queue: Approve, Edit, Reject |
| Act | Tell the patient, in their language | Telegram bot [D2-01-F9]; Indian speech APIs [D2-03-F58] | Telegram chat plus a web form |
| Learn | Improve choices from each patient's response | Personal drug-response trials [D2-03-F12]; adaptive message timing [D2-03-F10] | Roadmap only; nothing learns tonight |

Two Omron Connect models are encrypted [D1-06-F07]. Web Bluetooth needs HTTPS and a user click and is marked experimental [D1-06-F46].

**Reading any cuff's screen from a photo.** A purpose-trained reader reached mean errors of 1.2/0.8 mmHg on 776 US images and 0.9/0.5 mmHg on 1,934 Guatemalan recordings, against 4.1/2.7 mmHg for human transcribers on the Guatemalan set [D2-02-F4]. But 82% of 7,205 images in another Guatemalan set were poor quality, errors sat in the last digit, and only Omron screens were tested [D2-02-F4]. The open tool ssocr reads one row of digits [D2-02-F7]; 0 and 8, 1 and 7 get confused (search summary only) [D2-02-F9]. No published test of a general vision-language model on these screens was found [D2-02-F8].

**Blood pressure without a cuff, as of 2026.** The FDA cleared the Aktiia G0 cuffless monitor on 2 Jul 2025 [D2-02-F23]. The ESH says there are "no generally accepted protocols" for validating such devices [D2-02-F25], and a 2025 review found "no compelling evidence" of added value from pulse-wave methods [D2-02-F26]. A cuff must agree within a mean of 5 mmHg, SD up to 8 (search summary only) [D2-02-F27]. OUR VIEW: cuffless error is about the size of a dose step, and a kit version cannot be validated by noon. Do not build it tonight. Cuffless sensing stays on the roadmap until a validation protocol exists (chapter 5).

### C3. Making a home reading trustworthy

A home reading can be several mmHg wrong for reasons unrelated to the cuff. This section gives the guidance, the size of each mistake, the home threshold, and the clip that catches what a sensor can see.

**The guidance.** AHA: at least 5 minutes of quiet seated rest, two readings at least 1 minute apart, morning before tablets and evening, 7 days or more (minimum 3) [D2-02-F10]. ESH: the same, "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-02-F11, D2-01-F1]. Dropping day 1 is "a matter of debate" for the ESH [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10]. The ESH warns monitors over 4 years old drift [D2-02-F13] and calls handwritten logs "often incomplete and inaccurate" [D2-02-F14].

**The size of each mistake** (systolic / diastolic, mmHg):

| Mistake | Effect | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Arm on lap instead of on a desk | +3.9 / +4.0 (randomised crossover, n = 133, Baltimore) | [D2-02-F16] |
| Arm hanging at the side | +6.5 / +4.4 (same trial) | [D2-02-F16] |
| Arm below heart level | +0.49 / +0.47 per cm; arm at desk height against heart height +6.1 / +5.7 (n = 128) | [D2-02-F17] |
| Back not supported | +5 to +15 / +6 (AHA); +6 to +10 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F18, D2-02-F20] |
| Legs crossed | +5 to +8 / +3 to +5 | [D2-02-F18] |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs a large one | +4.8 systolic (randomised crossover, n = 195) | [D2-02-F19] |
| Regular cuff on an arm that needs an extra-large one | +19.5 systolic | [D2-02-F19] |
| Talking | +10 / +10 (older table, no citations in it) | [D2-02-F20] |
| Cuff over clothing | +5 to +50 systolic (older table) | [D2-02-F20] |
| No rest instead of 5 minutes | No meaningful difference below 140 systolic; none to at least 4 mmHg above (secondary review) | [D2-02-F21] |

The HEM-7120 standard cuff fits arms of 22-32 cm [D2-02-F30], so arm size must be measured.

**Home against clinic thresholds.** The ESH says a home mean of 135/85 corresponds to 140/90 in clinic [D2-01-F1]; the ISH [D2-01-F3] and the Indian Guidelines on Hypertension IV (search summary only) [D2-01-F4] use 135/85 at home. The Gujarat protocol is written for clinic readings at 140/90 [D1-06-F14]. Our engine (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-01-F1]) reads home sessions on days 24-30 of each 30-day cycle and calls a block "still high" at a home mean of 135 or 85; the full reading rule, with its minimum number of valid days, the day-1 rule and the urgent line, is in Appendix G. Using a clinic protocol on home readings is our choice and must be said on the slide.

Why it matters: SMARThealth India (stepped-wedge cluster trial, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh) found no blood-pressure effect, partly because "fluctuating BP values" made risk scores disagree, so only 37.2% of the cohort was exposed [D2-03-F17].

**The kit-built quality clip** (OUR DESIGN, from [D2-02-F10, D2-02-F16, D2-02-F17]; the picture is in chapter 4, the wiring and parts in Appendix G). An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff and the forearm. A helper seats the person correctly once and the clip stores that posture. It then:
- enforces 300 seconds of still rest, restarting on movement;
- checks the forearm is within 20 degrees of flat (a hanging arm fails) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of the stored posture;
- requires stillness through a 60-second measurement;
- enforces 60 seconds between readings.

A 15-degree change moves the cuff about 2.4 cm, about 1.2 mmHg (OUR ARITHMETIC: 15 x (0.866 - 0.707) = 2.4 cm; 2.4 x 0.49 = 1.2). The clip shows green or red and posts reasons, joined to the reading by time. It does not measure blood pressure. Legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking, bladder and smoking go into a 4-question phone checklist. Thresholds are OUR ESTIMATE. A weighted reading-quality score instead of pass or fail is roadmap work (chapter 5).

### C4. Algorithms that set a dose

Four families of dose algorithm are in use; each is bounded. The trials behind them are described in full in Appendix B; this section is about how each algorithm limits what it can do.

**Closed-loop insulin, the model case.** In trials, Control-IQ raised time in the target glucose range by 11 points against a sensor-augmented pump in type 1 diabetes [D1-01-F24], and 2IQP cut HbA1c (a blood test showing average sugar over about three months) a further 0.6 points in insulin-treated type 2 diabetes [D1-01-F43]. The do-it-yourself system OpenAPS writes its safety rules down [D2-03-F46]:
- It acts only through temporary basal rates, so if it stops, the pump returns to the normal plan; the core version "cannot issue insulin boluses".
- The temporary rate is capped by the lowest of several limits, including "4x the current scheduled basal rate".
- Missing or conflicting data sends it back to the pre-set plan.

Its code (oref0, MIT) says it is "not a 'set and forget' system" [D1-06-F12]; dosing logic sits in `determine-basal.js` [D1-06-F53].

**Insulin titration rules.** ADA 2025: start basal insulin at 10 units a day or 0.1-0.2 units/kg, "increase 2 units every 3 days to reach FPG target without hypoglycemia", and if low sugar has no clear reason "lower dose by 10-20%" [D1-06-F16]. An upper limit of 0.5 units/kg/day is quoted (search summary only) [D1-06-F18]. India's ICMR workflow gives targets but no titration schedule [D1-06-F17]. In trials, d-Nav (device plus clinician) cut HbA1c 1.0% against 0.3% for the clinician alone [D1-01-F13], and TeleDiab-2 cut it 1.44% and 1.48% against 0.92% [D1-01-F14]. The FDA has cleared dose apps such as My Dose Coach (2017) and iSage Rx (2024) [D2-03-F47]. A reinforcement-learning model, RL-DITR, was tested only single-arm in 16 inpatients in China [D2-03-F11].

**Blood-pressure protocols.** Gujarat's published ladder, with 30-day reviews: amlodipine 5 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, add telmisartan 40 mg, telmisartan 80 mg (after blood sugar, urea, creatinine and urine protein; if any is abnormal, refer, or, with no specialist reachable, withdraw telmisartan and add chlorthalidone), add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, then check adherence and refer. The sheet covers adults over 30, checks adherence at each visit, and bars telmisartan and chlorthalidone in pregnancy and in women of childbearing age not on effective contraception [D1-06-F14]. (How this sheet is written as a data file is in Appendix G.) Punjab and Maharashtra differ at step 2 [D1-06-F01, D1-06-F02]; across 159,292 patients who returned and stayed on protocol, control on clinic readings plateaued at 77% and 82% [D1-06-F04].

People do differ. PHYSIC (randomised, double-blind, repeated crossover, 280 people, Sweden, 1,468 treatment periods) found real between-person differences in drug response, worth about 4.4 mmHg if chosen per person [D2-03-F12]. A one-time "responder" label from a short run-in did not predict 12-month response in 608 Chinese patients [D2-03-F13].

**Warfarin tables.** The IWPC algorithm sets only the starting dose [D2-03-F48]. Feedback tables agree on no change at INR (a clotting test) 2.0-3.0 but differ outside it (search summary only) [D1-06-F37]. Self-management cut clots (RR 0.47) and deaths (RR 0.55) in pooled trials, compared indirectly with self-testing [D1-02-F05].

| Algorithm | Input | Output | How it is bounded |
|---|---|---|---|
| Closed-loop insulin | Continuous glucose sensor | Temporary basal rate | Rate caps, no boluses (oref0), revert on missing data [D2-03-F46] |
| Basal titration | Fasting glucose over 3 days | +2 units or -10-20% | Upper limit per kg; hypo branch; clinician sets cause [D1-06-F16, D1-06-F18] |
| BP ladder | 30-day review of readings | Next written regimen | Fixed steps, lab and pregnancy guards, referral at the end [D1-06-F14] |
| Warfarin table | INR | Weekly dose change in % | No-change band 2.0-3.0; hold at high INR [D1-06-F37] |

### C5. A protocol as data

A protocol written as data, not code, can be read by a clinician, tested branch by branch, and swapped without changing the engine. This section gives the prior art, what Indian decision-support trials found, the test-coverage lesson, and how our files fit.

**Prior art.**
- A 2002 review of 11 guideline languages found four basic parts: data collection, decision, patient state, intervention [D2-03-F54].
- WHO SMART Guidelines have no general hypertension kit; the blood-pressure kit is for pregnancy only, its machine-readable layers are "not yet available", and its licence is non-commercial [D2-03-F50, D2-03-F51].
- HL7 CQL is a standard logic language with an Apache-2.0 engine that is "not a complete implementation" and needs a Java 17 translator [D2-03-F52].
- CDS Hooks returns suggestion cards with an accept button (CC BY 4.0) [D2-03-F53].
- India's open Simple app (MIT, alive 4 Nov 2026) stores a protocol as a drug list plus `follow_up_days`; no step logic was found in its protocol model (Appendix D2) [D1-06-F40].

**Indian decision-support trials.**

| Trial | Design and setting | Compared | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| CARRS [D2-03-F14] | Randomised, 1,146 with diabetes, urban clinics, India and Pakistan, 28 months | Coordinators plus decision-support records against usual care | Positive: composite goal 18.2% against 8.1% |
| mWellcare [D2-03-F15] | Cluster randomised, 40 health centres, 3,698 people, 12 months | Nurse-run app with decision support against enhanced usual care | Null: systolic -0.98 (95% CI -4.64 to 2.67) |
| mPower Heart [D2-03-F16] | Before-and-after, no control, Himachal Pradesh, 6,797 people | Phone tool drafts prescription, physician vets | Systolic -14.6 mmHg, uncontrolled |
| SMARThealth India [D2-03-F17] | Stepped-wedge cluster, 18 clusters, rural Andhra Pradesh | Health-worker tablet plus doctor decision support against usual care | Null on blood pressure |
| IMPACT Diabetes [D2-03-F18] | Cluster randomised, 8 centres, 418 people, 9 months | Health-worker decision support under physician supervision | Small positive: HbA1c fall of 0.5% or more, 21.8% against 10.3% |

**The test-coverage lesson.** When the US VA re-encoded its hypertension decision support (ATHENA-HTN), 26 decision points gave 3,120 possible outputs, and 100 test cases covered "only 1% of the possible output combinations" [D2-03-F55].

**How our files fit** (OUR DESIGN; the files, the decision steps and the test table are in Appendix G). One YAML file per protocol: Gujarat, Nigeria, and the ADA insulin rule as paper only [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15, D1-06-F16]. Each number carries the exact source words; a missing value is `null` and the engine refuses that branch. A pure `decide()` function checks safety first, then enough readings, the 30-day interval, the threshold, adherence, the last step, and the lab and pregnancy guards, and only then proposes a step. It never computes a dose; it only picks a regimen written in the file. Thirty-six test cases cover every branch listed so far, run against two protocols; the age, childbearing-age, abnormal-lab and "outside the demo" branches found later on the sheets still need tests [D1-06-F14, D1-06-F15]. Insulin and heart-failure protocols in the same engine are roadmap work, and heart failure needs lab values (chapter 5).

### C6. Language models and medicine doses

Language models make dose errors even when told to follow a protocol.

| Study | Setup | Error |
|---|---|---|
| TacroDose AI [D2-03-F38] | GPT-4 prompted with a hospital tacrolimus protocol, 300 simulated cases | First version: 13.9% "sentinel errors"; with stronger constraints and output checks: 1.0%, and 13.3% of runs not reproducible (OUR ARITHMETIC: 100 - 86.7) |
| Anticoagulant hold times [D2-03-F39] | ChatGPT and Gemini, 25 cases | "potentially dangerous recommendations in 12-20% of scenarios" |
| Prescribing-error checker [D2-03-F40] | Randomised crossover, 91 error scenarios | Pharmacist plus model was best, 61% accuracy; 1.5 times better than the pharmacist alone at catching serious errors |
| Incident-report classification [D2-03-F41] | o4-mini, 200 Swedish reports | 96.0% agreement with pharmacists |

No completed randomised trial of a language-model coach with a blood-pressure or HbA1c outcome was found; two are registered [D2-03-F44], and an Indian trial protocol uses a frozen Mistral-7B with nurses after heart surgery [D2-03-F37].

**The design pattern** (OUR VIEW, following [D2-03-F38, D2-03-F40, D2-03-F46]):
1. The model handles language only: cuff photo to strict JSON, translation, speech.
2. A fixed, tested engine makes every decision, from the protocol file.
3. Code checks every output against the protocol: plausible ranges, two agreeing reads, a regimen that exists in the file.
4. A clinician approves every change.

**Indian-language tools.** Indian-language voice and offline speech models are roadmap work (chapter 5); tonight needs only a voice message.

### C8. Adaptive nudging, bandits and reinforcement learning (later work)

Adaptive nudging learns when and what to send each person. A just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) adapts "weekly, daily, or even many times a day"; a micro-randomised trial randomises each decision point [D2-03-F01]. Bandit timing of reminders, to help complete reading blocks, is roadmap work (chapter 5).

| Study | Design | Result |
|---|---|---|
| HeartSteps V1 [D2-03-F02] | Micro-randomised, 44 US adults, 6 weeks | Any suggestion +35 steps in 30 minutes (p = .06), fading over time; walking suggestions +59 (p = .02) |
| HeartSteps V2 [D2-03-F03]; Oralytics [D2-03-F08] | Learning algorithms deployed in US trials | Outcome results NOT FOUND |
| DIAMANTE [D2-03-F10] | Randomised, 3 arms, 168 people with diabetes and depression, US safety-net clinics, 6 months | Learned texts beat random texts: steps up 19% against 1.6% (random) and 3.9% (weekly message); HbA1c not in the abstract |
| Automated diabetes prevention app [D2-03-F42] | Randomised non-inferiority, 368 people, 2 US sites, 12 months | Matched human coaches: 31.7% against 31.9% |
| JITAI meta-analyses [D2-03-F04, D2-03-F06] | Mental health, 23 studies; sleep, 11 trials | Small effect (g = 0.15); adaptive not better than non-adaptive for sleep |

Two cautions. Standard estimators "can be inconsistent and fail to be replicable" on bandit-trial data [D2-03-F09]. A 2026 guideline for live learning systems uses pre-set fallbacks, which "safeguarded participants" in two case studies [D2-03-F07].

Open tools: MABWiser (Apache 2.0) [D1-06-F55]; Open Bandit Pipeline (Apache 2.0, off-policy estimators) [D2-03-F49]; HeartSteps V1 data (CC BY 4.0, 8,274 decisions) [D1-06-F44].

### C9. Personal response models and "digital twins" (later work)

A "digital twin" here is a model of one person that predicts their response to food or treatment. A model of each patient's response to the next step, built from real approved steps, is roadmap work (chapter 5). Twin Health as a company (funding, prices, Indian presence) is in Appendix D.

- **Twin Health, India, blood pressure** [D2-03-F19]: secondary analysis of an Indian randomised trial in 319 people with type 2 diabetes (233 twin, 86 standard care). Home readings guided blood-pressure drug changes. Systolic fell 7.6 against 3.2 mmHg at one year. Limits: secondary analysis, only 59 people on blood-pressure drugs, company-linked. The drug changes followed a protocol; the machine learning predicted diet response.
- **Method** [D2-03-F21]: predicts each person's post-meal glucose from a glucose sensor, food logs and other inputs and "dynamically adjusts dietary recommendations". No open code found.
- **Twin Health, US** [D2-03-F43]: randomised, 150 people, Cleveland Clinic, 12 months; HbA1c under 6.5% without glucose drugs other than metformin in 71% against 2.4%. Source is the institution's summary; funding not shown.
- **Twin Health, real world** [D2-03-F20]: 1,853 completers, HbA1c -1.8%, no control (THEIR CLAIM).
- **Glucose foundation models**: GluFormer (over 10 million readings, 10,812 adults) predicted later diabetes and cardiovascular death (arXiv only) [D2-03-F23]; CGM-LSM and GlucoFM report lower forecast error [D2-03-F24].
- **Blood pressure**: one agent-based model simulates six drugs on virtual patients; licence unconfirmed (search summary only) [D1-06-F43].

PHYSIC measured personal response over repeated periods [D2-03-F12]; a single run-in response did not predict the long-term one [D2-03-F13] (both in C4).

### C12. So what for us

OUR VIEW.
- **The reading is the science.** Arm position alone adds 3.9-6.5 mmHg [D2-02-F16], and noisy readings broke an Indian trial [D2-03-F17]. The clip and reading rules are our deep-tech claim, not the rules engine. The engine refuses to step a dose on readings that fail the clip, so a posture mistake costs a repeat, not a wrong prescription.
- **Blood pressure is the signal to start with.** It is the one signal a household can measure tonight with a validated, cheap device. The photo path reaches any cuff, so we do not depend on Bluetooth, but every photo read must be shown back to the patient to confirm.
- **Join open parts, with a safety rule at each handover.** Every stage of the loop has open parts and none needs a new model tonight; the value is in joining them.
- **Bound every action.** Every working dose algorithm caps its actions and falls back to a standing plan when data is missing; a ladder is the simplest case. Copy OpenAPS [D2-03-F46]: choose only written regimens, hold the current step on missing data, never step on one reading.
- **Keep models on language.** A 1% dangerous-error rate under the best constraints [D2-03-F38] rules out a model choosing doses. The model reads photos and speaks Hindi; the engine decides. Sarvam is the fastest way to a Hindi voice message tonight; the MIT models are the path to running offline later. Of the frontier-lab models, only MedGemma, PaPaGei and HealthBench can be downloaded, none sets doses, and nothing from them enters our decision.
- **Act between visits, not during them.** Decision support used during clinic visits did not beat good usual care in two Indian trials [D2-03-F15, D2-03-F17]; our value is the change made without a visit.
- **Test on generated cases and replayed data, not only hand-written ones.** ATHENA's 1% coverage says so [D2-03-F55]. Our honest tests tonight are branch coverage, a replay of the `bp` Ghana data, and a labelled simulated cohort calibrated to the IHCI step curve.
- **The learning layer is earned, not claimed.** People do respond differently to drugs [D2-03-F12], which is the honest reason a later learning layer could add value, but no open twin exists for blood-pressure drugs. Each approved step in our loop gives one labelled example (readings before, readings 30 days after); that is the dataset a response model would need, and it does not exist in the open today [D1-06-F42]. Adaptive timing has one head-to-head win, on steps, not a clinical measure; in our loop it could help complete 7-day reading blocks, later, and a HeartSteps replay shows the method only.
